original_supporting_findings.finding_label: BHMT remethylates homocysteine with betaine and catalytic zinc
original_supporting_findings.finding_summary: Human betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT) transfers one methyl group from betaine to homocysteine. The products are methionine and dimethylglycine. A zinc ion bound by three cysteines activates homocysteine. Folate and vitamin B12 are not part of this reaction.
original_supporting_findings.finding_interpretation: This is the reaction boundary. It does not include folate-dependent remethylation, the later conversion of methionine to SAMe, whole-cycle throughput, phosphatidylethanolamine methyltransferase, or acetylcholine formation. It also does not show that dietary zinc intake changes the reaction in people.
original_supporting_findings.finding_statement: BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, forming methionine and dimethylglycine, without folate or vitamin B12 in that reaction, and uses an active-site zinc ion to activate homocysteine.
original_supporting_findings.synthesis: Human crystal structures show that BHMT makes methionine from betaine and homocysteine and uses zinc to activate homocysteine. Mutating any of the three zinc-binding cysteines to alanine abolishes activity and sharply reduces zinc binding, and the same biochemical work states the products as methionine and dimethylglycine. A methyl-donor review states that methyl flow through this pathway does not depend on folate or vitamin B12. Together these sources identify the reaction and its metal. They do not test ordinary dietary control or human tissue flux.
original_supporting_findings.synthesis_limitations: The enzyme evidence uses purified or recombinant human protein, not intact human metabolism. Loss of activity after removing zinc ligands does not show that dietary zinc usually limits the enzyme. The review statement that the pathway is independent of folate and vitamin B12 is not a new flux experiment. Quantitative claims in that review about choline deficiency and liver methionine were not re-checked in the primary animal papers.

evidence_considered.label: Evans et al. (2002)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Human BHMT structures show methionine formation from betaine and homocysteine, with zinc activating homocysteine; oxidation that expels zinc rearranges the active site.

assessment.study: X-ray structures of human BHMT in an oxidised zinc-free form and a reduced zinc-bound form with a homocysteine-like bisubstrate analog.
assessment.population: Purified crystallised human BHMT; no cells, animals or human participants.
assessment.result: The enzyme forms methionine from betaine and homocysteine. Zinc activates homocysteine. The zinc-binding sequences sit at the ends of barrel strands, and a Cys217–Cys299 disulfide expels zinc.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Structures at 2.15 Å (zinc-free) and 2.05 Å (zinc-bound). No physiological effect size applies.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct structural evidence for the human reaction and for catalytic zinc.
assessment.limitations: Static structures establish catalytic geometry, not in-vivo flux, dietary zinc responsiveness, or a clinical outcome.

evidence_considered.label: Breksa and Garrow (1999)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Replacing any of Cys217, Cys299 or Cys300 with alanine abolished human BHMT activity and reduced zinc binding. The reaction produces methionine and dimethylglycine from betaine and homocysteine.

assessment.study: Site-directed mutagenesis of recombinant human liver BHMT, with activity and zinc-binding measurements.
assessment.population: Recombinant human BHMT protein expressed in bacteria; no human participants.
assessment.result: Cys217, Cys299 and Cys300 were identified as zinc ligands. Mutation of any one to alanine caused complete loss of activity and a significant reduction in zinc binding. The catalysed transfer is from betaine to homocysteine, yielding dimethylglycine and methionine.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Complete loss of activity for each alanine substitution. No human effect size applies.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct evidence that catalytic activity of human BHMT depends on those zinc ligands, and a clear statement of the reaction products.
assessment.limitations: Bacterial expression and purified-protein assays do not show that dietary zinc limits BHMT in human tissues.

evidence_considered.label: Obeid (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Methyl-group flow through BHMT does not depend on folate or vitamin B12, although the pathway is most active in liver and kidney and talks to the folate route.

assessment.study: Narrative review of methyl-donor deficiency with emphasis on the BHMT pathway.
assessment.population: Review of human and animal methyl-donor studies; not a new experiment.
assessment.result: BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine. The review states that methyl flow through this pathway is not dependent on folate or vitamin B12, while several cross-talk mechanisms exist. BHMT is particularly active in liver and kidney.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No new effect size. The review cites other studies for homocysteine and metabolite changes.
assessment.evidence_summary: Explicit pathway-level statement that folate and vitamin B12 are not required for methyl flow through BHMT.
assessment.limitations: A review cannot replace a flux assay. Some quantitative deficiency claims are attributed to other papers and were not re-adjudicated here.

evidence_dependency: Obeid (2013) is also primary evidence in PM2-F2 for choline oxidation. That reuse is one review, not a second experiment.

original_supporting_findings.finding_label: Choline oxidation supplies betaine and is not the BHMT reaction
original_supporting_findings.finding_summary: Choline can be oxidised to betaine aldehyde and then to betaine. That sequence can supply the BHMT substrate. It is not the methyl transfer that BHMT carries out, and betaine is not turned back into choline.
original_supporting_findings.finding_interpretation: Choline is a precursor of the substrate, not a cofactor or substrate of BHMT. Acetylcholine formation and phosphatidylethanolamine methylation use choline or SAMe in other reactions.
original_supporting_findings.finding_statement: Irreversible oxidation of choline to betaine is an upstream supply route for the BHMT substrate and is not itself the BHMT reaction.
original_supporting_findings.synthesis: A methyl-donor review states that betaine is produced by irreversible oxidation of choline through choline dehydrogenase and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, and that BHMT then uses betaine. A choline-dehydrogenase review places the human enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane, mainly in kidney and liver, and separates the first oxidation to betaine aldehyde from the second oxidation to betaine. Betaine then donates a methyl group in the homocysteine-to-methionine reaction. The two steps are supply, not the BHMT reaction.
original_supporting_findings.synthesis_limitations: Purified, stable human choline dehydrogenase has been difficult to obtain, so some catalytic detail is inferred from related enzymes and from tissue activity rather than from a complete human kinetic characterisation. The reviews do not show that raising choline intake increases BHMT flux in people.

evidence_considered.directional_finding: Betaine can be formed by irreversible oxidation of choline via choline dehydrogenase and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, and BHMT then uses that betaine to remethylate homocysteine.

assessment.study: Narrative review of methyl-donor metabolism centred on BHMT.
assessment.population: Review of human and animal evidence; not a new enzyme assay.
assessment.result: The review states the two-enzyme oxidation of choline to betaine and the subsequent BHMT reaction. It treats the oxidation as irreversible.
assessment.effect_magnitude: No new effect size for the oxidation steps.
assessment.evidence_summary: Pathway-level evidence that choline oxidation supplies betaine upstream of BHMT.
assessment.limitations: Review synthesis, not a direct demonstration of human choline dehydrogenase kinetics or of dietary choline increasing BHMT flux.

evidence_considered.label: Salvi and Gadda (2013)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Human choline dehydrogenase oxidises choline to betaine aldehyde, and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase completes formation of betaine, which can donate a methyl group to homocysteine.

assessment.study: Review of human choline dehydrogenase localisation, physiological role and biochemical characterisation.
assessment.population: Review of human tissue activity and comparative biochemistry; not a dietary trial.
assessment.result: The enzyme sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is found mainly in kidney and liver. It oxidises choline to betaine aldehyde. A second enzyme, betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, oxidises that aldehyde to betaine. Betaine is described as a methyl donor for methionine formation from homocysteine. Purified active human enzyme has been difficult to obtain.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Tissue activity was reported mainly in kidney, with about six-fold lower activity in liver. No dietary dose-response was measured.
assessment.evidence_summary: Enzyme-level support for the two-step oxidation that supplies betaine.
assessment.limitations: Incomplete purification of human choline dehydrogenase limits kinetic detail. Localisation and pathway role do not show that dietary choline changes BHMT flux.

evidence_dependency: Obeid (2013) is also primary evidence in PM2-F1 for folate- and vitamin B12-independence of BHMT. That reuse is one review, not a second experiment.

original_supporting_findings.finding_summary: Methionine becomes SAM, SAM donates a methyl group, and SAH is hydrolysed to homocysteine. Homocysteine is then either remethylated to methionine or sent into transsulfuration toward cysteine.
original_supporting_findings.finding_interpretation: This is the integrated route and the branch. It does not assign the MAT, remethylation or transsulfuration reactions to this mechanism, and it does not show that ordinary diet changes the rates.
original_supporting_findings.finding_statement: Methionine-cycle throughput runs from methionine to SAM, methyl transfer and SAH hydrolysis to homocysteine, after which homocysteine is distributed between remethylation and transsulfuration under the influence of SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate.
original_supporting_findings.synthesis: A methylation review establishes SAM as the methyl donor and SAH hydrolysis to adenosine and homocysteine, and it shows that blocking that hydrolysis can affect methylation of phospholipids, proteins, DNA, RNA and small molecules together. A pathway review then places regulation at the distribution of homocysteine between remethylation, which every tissue can perform, and transsulfuration to cystathionine, which is limited to liver, kidney, small intestine and pancreas, with SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate as effectors. original_supporting_findings.finding_summary: Removing both methionine and cysteine slowed whole-blood glutathione synthesis in healthy young men. Combined cysteine-precursor and glycine supplementation raised erythrocyte synthesis in older adults. A methionine-adequate diet without cysteine did not lower erythrocyte synthesis in young men.
original_supporting_findings.finding_interpretation: Substrate supply can change blood-cell synthesis in these specific conditions. That does not mean every ordinary diet is cysteine-limited, and the older-adult result is a supplemental precursor plus glycine, not a food prescription.
original_supporting_findings.finding_statement: Human blood-cell glutathione synthesis can slow when dietary methionine and cysteine are both removed and can rise in older adults after combined cysteine and glycine precursor supplementation, whereas a methionine-adequate cysteine-free diet did not limit erythrocyte synthesis in young men.
original_supporting_findings.synthesis: Three human tracer studies set the ceiling. In seven healthy young men, a 10-day amino-acid diet with methionine and cysteine removed lowered whole-blood fractional synthesis from 0.65 ± 0.13 to 0.49 ± 0.13 per day and lowered absolute synthesis by about 23%, while concentration stayed near 1.2 mM and glycine intake was not reduced. In eight older adults compared with eight younger adults, erythrocyte glutathione synthesis and concentration were lower, and two weeks of cysteine plus glycine precursor supplementation raised fractional synthesis by 78.8% and absolute synthesis by 230.9%. The cysteine source in that protocol is N-acetylcysteine, given with glycine. In four young men, cysteine intakes from zero to 40 mg/kg/day did not change erythrocyte synthesis when methionine was held at 14 mg/kg/day. Synthesis is therefore substrate-responsive under defined restrictions, not universally limited by dietary cysteine.
original_supporting_findings.synthesis_limitations: All three studies measured blood-cell, not neuronal, synthesis. The sulfur-amino-acid-free diet was an experimental amino-acid formula in seven young men for 10 days. The older-adult increase required combined supplementation and was not an isolated N-acetylcysteine or glycine test, not an ADHD trial, and not ordinary food. The cysteine-free arm used only four young men and two days of adaptation. Concentration did not track synthesis rate in the sulfur-amino-acid-free study.

evidence_considered.label: Lyons et al. (2000)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: A sulfur-amino-acid-free amino-acid diet slowed whole-blood glutathione synthesis in healthy young men without lowering glutathione concentration.

assessment.study: Randomised crossover of two 10-day L-amino-acid diets, adequate versus methionine and cysteine both set to zero, with a primed intravenous L-[1-13C]cysteine infusion on day 10.
assessment.population: Seven healthy men, age 24 ± 6 years.
assessment.result: Fractional synthesis fell from 0.65 ± 0.13 to 0.49 ± 0.13 per day (P < 0.01). Absolute synthesis fell from 747 ± 216 to 578.6 ± 135 µmol/L/day (P < 0.05), about 23%. Whole-blood glutathione stayed about 1.2 mM (1,142 ± 243 versus 1,216 ± 162 µM). Glycine in the formula rose from 39.6 to 75.1 mg/kg/day so nitrogen stayed constant; glutamic acid was unchanged.
assessment.effect_magnitude: About a 23% lower absolute synthesis rate after 10 days without methionine and cysteine; concentration unchanged.
assessment.evidence_summary: Direct human evidence that removing the shared sulfur-amino-acid supply slows whole-blood glutathione synthesis.
assessment.limitations: Experimental formula, young men, short duration, whole blood rather than brain, and no clinical outcome. Glycine was increased, so the slowdown is not a glycine deficit.

evidence_considered.label: Sekhar et al. (2011)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Older adults had lower erythrocyte glutathione synthesis than younger adults, and two weeks of cysteine plus glycine precursor supplementation restored synthesis and concentration.

assessment.study: Stable-isotope erythrocyte glutathione kinetics before and after precursor supplementation. Cysteine was supplied as N-acetylcysteine together with glycine.
assessment.population: Eight older adults restudied after supplementation, compared with eight younger adults.
assessment.result: Before supplementation, older adults had lower erythrocyte glycine, cysteine, glutathione concentration, fractional synthesis (45.80 ± 5.69 versus 83.14 ± 6.43 %/day) and absolute synthesis (0.55 ± 0.12 versus 1.73 ± 0.16 mmol/L red cells per day). After two weeks, glutathione concentration was 94.6% higher, fractional synthesis 78.8% higher and absolute synthesis 230.9% higher, and plasma oxidative-stress markers were lower.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Combined precursor supplementation in older adults: fractional synthesis +78.8% and absolute synthesis +230.9% from the deficient baseline.
assessment.evidence_summary: Human evidence that combined supplemental cysteine precursor and glycine can raise erythrocyte glutathione synthesis when it is low in older adults.
assessment.limitations: Small older-adult sample, erythrocyte pool, combined supplements, not ordinary food, not neuronal synthesis, and not an ADHD or recovery trial.

evidence_considered.label: Courtney-Martin et al. (2008)
evidence_considered.directional_finding: Erythrocyte glutathione synthesis did not change across cysteine intakes, including zero, when methionine intake was adequate.

assessment.study: Five graded cysteine intakes (0, 10, 20, 30 and 40 mg/kg/day) in random order with methionine fixed at 14 mg/kg/day and protein at 1 g/kg/day. Erythrocyte glutathione synthesis was measured after two days at each intake.
assessment.population: Four healthy young adult men.
assessment.result: Fractional and absolute erythrocyte glutathione synthesis and glutathione concentration did not change as cysteine intake increased. Urinary sulfate excretion rose with cysteine intake (r = 0.92).
assessment.effect_magnitude: No change in erythrocyte glutathione synthesis across the cysteine range tested.
assessment.evidence_summary: Human evidence that dietary cysteine is not independently limiting for erythrocyte glutathione synthesis when methionine intake meets the protein requirement.
assessment.limitations: Preliminary sample of four men, two-day adaptation, erythrocyte endpoint, and no neuronal or clinical outcome.

evidence_dependency: Sekhar et al. (2011) is also used in PM6-F3 and PM6-F4 for the phenome boundary, and in PM6-IC1 for the measurement boundary. Those uses are not independent replications of the synthesis-rate result.
